theme: Clarity, legitimacy & knowing when not to play · 드러켄밀러의 '쉬는 판단'과 중국의 정당성

tracks.title: Stan Druckenmiller: Why he's 'not playing' right now (14 min)
tracks.show: Morgan Stanley · TomorrowX Summit, with Iliana Bouzali (Nov 17, 2026)

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: I can't remember a period where I had less clarity on where we're going to be in 12 months.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: Who's going to compete with these guys in cyber security?

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: You have the biggest thing going on in the history of American visits.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: I think we're going to beat cancer.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: I think it's going to be a managed disease.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: And I mean in 10 years, not 20 years.

transcript.speaker: Iliana Bouzali
transcript.text: It's auto reply.

transcript.text: Hi, Stan.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: Hello, Eliana.

transcript.speaker: Iliana Bouzali
transcript.text: Gavin, thanks for giving us an excuse to do this again.

transcript.speaker: Iliana Bouzali
transcript.text: We did it about nine months ago.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: Before we start, I know we're time pressed, but I have to tell a little story about Ileana and Gavin.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: Ileana runs the global derivatives business at Morgan Stanley.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: And she has these Zoom calls for, back then, we were called macro legends.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: More appropriately, in my opinion, macro has-beens.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: But we had this Zoom call about a month after chat GPT.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: And all the macro legends were opining on interest rates and other matters.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: And this guy I'd never seen before, Gavin comes on the Zoom and he says, you guys all have your head up here, you know what?

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: And you have the biggest thing going on in the history of American business.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: And you're all here talking about nickels and dimes.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: And, Gavin, I want to thank you because that was right when it all started, and you predicted the whole thing, and you predicted the very of it, and I want to thank you, Ileana, because I would not have met Gavin if it weren't for you.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: So thank you both.

transcript.speaker: Iliana Bouzali
transcript.text: You're welcome.

transcript.speaker: Iliana Bouzali
transcript.text: So I went back to our January conversation, similar to this, a smaller audience, and When you were bullish the economy, you were long equities, you were short treasuries as a hedge, you were long copper, and you had this belief that healthcare was going to be a breakout winner.

transcript.speaker: Iliana Bouzali
transcript.text: So how much of that portfolio do you own today?

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: Basically almost none.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: And when I looked at January when you interviewed me, it was a unique time.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: Sometimes in my career I've had clarity, and sometimes I have no clarity.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: And when I have clarity, I like to play big, and when I don't have clarity, I'll almost sometimes not play.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: So at the time, if you'll recall, the economy was very strong.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: Now, more importantly, looking forward, Fed funds were three and a half, nominal growth was six percent, so monetary policy was ridiculously loose.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: And if you looked at the so-called Fed dot plot, more interest rate cuts were supposedly coming later in the year.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: Commodities were breaking out to a new high, including copper.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: The advanced decline line and other technicals I look at the market were all making new highs, credit spreads were very, very tight.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: So it seemed almost impossible to me that we could have a recession within six to 12 months and with overly stimulated monetary policy.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: And then there was another thing happening, which was Claude Code, the previous fall pretty late, had just kind of gotten everyone excited, excited, or let's say the insiders excited, about an acceleration in AI.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: So we were quite bullish on capital spending.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: So this all made us quite bullish equities, and as you said, the economy.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: Unfortunately, about a month later, something called a war started.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: I panicked.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: We sold a bunch of stuff, but I actually ended up lucky because when we brought it back, which we did quickly, it was more apparent than ever that AI infrastructure was going to have a complete liftoff.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: So it cleaned out all the stuff in the portfolio that wasn't going to be a big rise.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: So now let's look at today.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: The economy still is strong, but everything else I just talked about has completely flipped on its head.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: The Fed is not cutting, they're hiking.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: We've had regime change at the Fed, a gentleman I know while he sat next to me for 15 years.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: He is not happy that we had free money for 15 years while the deficit and everything else went through the roof.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: He's even less happy that inflation's been above target for five years.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: So we have monetary tightening going on.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: We have commodities, which were breaking out in January, looked like they topped and are going down.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: In fact, we're now short copper.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: The advanced decline line, which is making a new high when we were interviewed, made its high back on August 14, despite the fact the average is making their high in October.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: credit spreads are widening.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: I think you're getting the joke here.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: Everything is the exact opposite of the way it was then, so we are not long equities.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: We're not short equities.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: I like to go short, I admit it, but for all the reasons I think most people came to this conference, I wouldn't dare go short.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: The innovation and everything going on here.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: Also, a lot of that stuff is oversold and washed out and I think positions are down tactically so my choice here is to do what I've sort of always done when I don't have clarity and I've been doing this oh my god for 50 years I've been doing this I can't remember a period where I had less clarity on where we're going to be in 12 months unlike last January so as you made fun of me on one of these zoom calls the other day and you said,

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: What I've always done, because we are a matrix investor, the four categories I just mentioned, is I look at my P&L, and if it's not behaving the way it should be, if it's not correlating properly, I'll start cutting back.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: So the P&L is my true signal.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: Why do I think that's better in VAR?

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: People in Texas know sports.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
transcript.text: As you know in baseball, way beyond random you get streaks, hitting streaks, winning streaks.

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller

transcript.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller

tracks.note: Druckenmiller가 대부분 말해요(14분 중 약 11분, 진행자 Iliana Bouzali는 질문). 0:00–0:17 예고 몽타주 → 0:30 'macro has-beens'와 Gavin 이야기 → 2:09 1월엔 왜 강세였나 → 4:24 지금은 모든 게 뒤집혔다('I'm not playing') → 6:41 그의 기록과 4개 자산군 → 9:35 VaR 대신 P&L, 'streaks'(연속 안타) → 11:48 AI 'use cases', 'tasks instead of tokens'(14분에서 끊겨요). 스크립트는 자동 음성인식(whisper)이라 틀린 곳이 있어요: American visits = American business, Eliana/Ileana = Iliana, bare markets = bear markets, stress tax = stress tests, VAR = VaR(value at risk), quantum fund = Quantum Fund, economically disappointed = economically disappointing. 1회차는 흐름만, 2회차는 스크립트를 보면서 들어요.

listening.task: 오늘은 Stanley Druckenmiller의 Morgan Stanley TomorrowX Summit 대담(2026년 11월 17일) 앞부분 14분이에요. 진행자 Iliana Bouzali가 묻고 Druckenmiller가 길게 답해요. 출근길(8:30–9:00)에는 0:00–6:40(1월엔 왜 강세였나 → 지금은 모든 게 뒤집혀서 'I'm not playing')을 1배속(어려우면 0.75배속)으로 흐름만 듣고, 퇴근길(17:30–18:10)에는 6:40–14:00(4개 자산군, P&L이 신호, 야구의 'streaks', AI 'tasks instead of tokens')을 들어요. 시간이 남으면 처음부터 한 번 더! 'macro has-beens', 'flipped on its head', 'capital preservation', 'selling tasks instead of tokens'가 나오는 부분을 잘 들어 보세요. 바쁘면 Part 1의 처음 6분(~'That's where we are')만 들어도 OK예요.

quiz.q: Why is Druckenmiller 'not playing' right now? a) He lost a lot of money this year and is scared, b) He has very little clarity — the signals that made him bullish in January (loose Fed, rising commodities, tight credit spreads) have all flipped, c) He thinks AI is a bubble and wants to go short
quiz.answer: b) 1월에는 Fed가 완화적이고 원자재·기술적 지표가 좋아서 강세였지만, 지금은 Fed가 금리를 올리고, 원자재는 꺾이고, 신용 스프레드가 벌어지는 등 '모든 게 정반대'예요. 50년 중 12개월 뒤가 이렇게 안 보인 적이 없어서 쉬고 있대요. 숏(c)은 'I wouldn't dare go short'라고 했어요.

reading.title: Does a crummy economy threaten China’s social contract?
reading.source: The Economist (public reprint via Hindustan Times)
reading.summaryKo: 연말에 중국을 찾는 외국 방문객들은 '경제가 나빠졌으니 정치적 자유와 번영을 맞바꾼 중국의 사회계약이 깨진 것 아니냐'고 묻는대요. 칼럼은 정당성이 돈만의 문제가 아니라고 말해요: 치안·기차·올림픽 금메달, '100년 굴욕'을 끝낸 역사, 다른 나라의 혼란도 공산당 편이에요. 학자 Zhao Dingxin은 정당성을 절차·성과·이념 세 가지로 나누는데, 성과 정당성은 사람들이 계속 '더'를 원해서 본래 불안정하대요. 그래서 시진핑은 이념과 '강대국 지위'를 키우려 하고, 경제가 처져도 계약이 깨진 게 아니라 다른 지지 기반을 키우고 있다는 결론이에요.
excerpt: Many leave impressed by the slick modernity of China’s wealthiest cities. The more intrepid also see some rougher edges. Invited to chat with several delegations, Chaguan heard one question again and again. Visitors wanted to know whether China’s social contract was in tatters.

In the simplified version of the supposed Chinese social contract—the visitors’ version—the exchange is straightforward, even vulgar. You swap political rights for higher incomes. Legitimacy, by contrast, comes from multiple sources.
reading.tip: 'Chaguan'은 The Economist 중국 칼럼 이름(찻집)이라 칼럼니스트가 자신을 3인칭으로 불러요. 'in tatters'(누더기가 된 → 엉망이 된), 'the more intrepid'(더 대담한 사람들), 'by contrast'(대조적으로)를 보세요. 줄표(—the visitors’ version—)는 괄호처럼 '설명 끼워넣기'예요.

review.from: Jim Cramer · CNBC · Mad Money · 11/25 듣기
review.text: Because portfolio managers could go in easily and out easily, though, the futures became the most powerful drivers of stock prices, particularly for hedge funds, even more powerful than the actual forms of the underlying companies that stocks are meant to represent.
review.why: 주어(the futures)가 앞의 Because절과 though 뒤에 숨어 있어요. 'Because ~, though,' = '그런데 ~했기 때문에'. 대본의 'forms'는 실제로는 firms(기업)로 말한 거예요.
chunks: that stocks are meant to represent.
review.paraphrase: Fund managers could buy and sell futures quickly, so futures moved stock prices more than the real companies behind the stocks did.
review.ko: 펀드매니저들이 선물은 쉽게 사고팔 수 있었기 때문에, 선물이 주가를 움직이는 가장 큰 힘이 됐어요. 주식이 원래 대표하는 실제 기업들보다도 더 강하게요.

review.text: Now the buzz in India’s startup capital is “deep tech”—a somewhat loosely applied term for products supposedly based on scientific breakthroughs or advanced engineering in sectors like space, defence and semiconductors.
review.why: 대시(—) 뒤는 'deep tech'를 풀어 설명하는 부분이에요. buzz = 화제·유행어, loosely applied = 대충(느슨하게) 붙이는, supposedly = ~라고들 하는(의심 섞임).
chunks: in sectors like space, defence and semiconductors.
review.paraphrase: Today everyone in Bangalore is talking about “deep tech”, a vague label for products said to come from real science or advanced engineering, in areas like space, defence and chips.
review.ko: 요즘 인도 스타트업 수도(벵갈루루)의 화두는 '딥테크'예요. 우주·국방·반도체처럼 과학적 돌파나 첨단 공학에 기반한다고들 하는 제품에 꽤 느슨하게 붙이는 말이죠.

evening.note: 금요일이에요 🎉 지난번 읽은 데서 이어서 10페이지. 한 주 마무리라 피곤하면 5페이지만, 아니면 Minimum day도 OK.
